questions.stem: A hospitalized client with systemic inflammation, edema, poor intake, and a serum albumin of 2.5 g/dL is referred for nutrition assessment. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The albumin value confirms protein-calorie malnutrition by itself and can be used as the primary marker to quantify the severity of the client's nutrition deficit.","B":"The albumin value primarily measures recent protein intake, so normalization after several meals would reliably demonstrate that the client's nutrition deficit has resolved.","C":"The albumin value is unaffected by inflammation or capillary permeability, making it a specific marker of total body protein in acutely ill hospitalized clients.","D":"The low albumin is associated with inflammation and adverse-outcome risk but cannot diagnose malnutrition by itself; nutrition assessment must use clinical and intake data."}}
questions.rationale: ASPEN specifically advises that serum albumin and prealbumin should not be used as nutrition markers or proxy measures of total body protein. Their concentrations fall with inflammation and altered capillary permeability and are better interpreted as markers associated with illness severity and nutrition risk. Diagnosis of malnutrition requires broader clinical assessment.
questions.source_name: ASPEN — The Use of Visceral Proteins as Nutrition Markers: Position Paper
questions.source_detail: ASPEN states that albumin and prealbumin characterize inflammation rather than nutrition status and should not be used to diagnose protein-energy malnutrition.

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis becomes newly confused and has asterixis. The serum ammonia level is elevated. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's clinical reasoning?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The presentation is compatible with hepatic encephalopathy, but the diagnosis and severity are clinical; the ammonia value alone should not be used to grade or confirm the syndrome.","B":"The elevated ammonia concentration confirms both the diagnosis and the exact grade of hepatic encephalopathy, so no further assessment for other causes of confusion is needed.","C":"The ammonia result rules out hepatic encephalopathy because clinically important encephalopathy generally occurs only when ammonia values remain within the reference range.","D":"The serum ammonia value should determine the lactulose dose independently of neurologic findings, bowel response, precipitating factors, and the client's overall clinical course over time."}}
questions.rationale: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis. AASLD notes that ammonia levels do not consistently correlate with the presence or severity of encephalopathy and should not be used alone to rule in or grade HE. Other causes and precipitating factors for altered mental status still require assessment.
questions.source_detail: AASLD: ammonia levels do not consistently correlate with HE severity; HE remains a clinical diagnosis and alternative causes/precipitants should be evaluated.

questions.stem: A client reports fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, and weight gain. Laboratory testing shows a markedly elevated TSH. Which additional result would most strongly support primary hypothyroidism?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An elevated free T4 concentration, because primary hypothyroidism is characterized by increased pituitary TSH and increased circulating thyroid hormone.","B":"A low free T4 concentration, because elevated TSH together with reduced circulating free T4 is the classic biochemical pattern of primary hypothyroidism.","C":"A suppressed TSH on repeat testing, because primary hypothyroidism ordinarily causes simultaneous suppression of both TSH and circulating free thyroid hormone.","D":"An isolated elevated total T3 concentration, because T3 is the most reliable confirmatory test for primary hypothyroidism when the TSH is markedly increased."}}
questions.rationale: The American Thyroid Association describes elevated TSH with low free T4 (or free T4 index) as the typical biochemical pattern of primary hypothyroidism. T3 testing is much more useful in evaluating hyperthyroidism and may remain normal even in significant hypothyroidism.
questions.source_name: American Thyroid Association — Thyroid Function Tests
questions.source_detail: ATA: elevated TSH plus low FT4/FTI indicates primary hypothyroidism; T3 is not the preferred confirmatory test for hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A client with recurrent gout is taking urate-lowering therapy. Which laboratory goal best reflects the treat-to-target approach recommended for long-term gout management?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Maintain serum urate above the saturation range so existing crystals remain stable and additional inflammatory flares are less likely to occur.","B":"Use symptoms alone and avoid serial serum urate measurements because laboratory targets have no role once urate-lowering therapy has been started.","C":"Titrate urate-lowering therapy toward a serum urate target below 6 mg/dL while monitoring adherence, tolerability, and the client's clinical course.","D":"Stop urate-lowering therapy as soon as the first flare-free month occurs, because continuing treatment below a serum urate target increases crystal formation."}}
questions.rationale: The American College of Rheumatology gout guideline strongly supports a treat-to-target strategy for patients receiving urate-lowering therapy, with dose titration guided by serial serum urate and a target below 6 mg/dL. Urate-lowering therapy is long-term disease management, not something stopped after a brief flare-free period.
questions.source_name: American College of Rheumatology — 2020 Guideline for the Management of Gout
questions.source_detail: ACR recommends treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy with serial serum urate measurements and a target serum urate below 6 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has an elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin but no ischemic symptoms or new ECG changes. Which statement best reflects how the nurse should interpret this result?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Any troponin value above the reference limit establishes an acute myocardial infarction regardless of symptoms, ECG findings, serial change, or the clinical context.","B":"Troponin elevation identifies skeletal-muscle injury rather than myocardial injury, so the result has little relevance when the client has chronic kidney disease.","C":"A single elevated troponin rules out acute coronary syndrome because myocardial infarction requires troponin values to remain within the reference interval.","D":"Troponin elevation indicates myocardial injury, but myocardial infarction requires clinical evidence of acute ischemia and interpretation of the pattern in context."}}
questions.rationale: Cardiac troponin above the 99th-percentile reference limit establishes myocardial injury, not automatically myocardial infarction. The universal definition of MI requires integration of a rise/fall pattern when appropriate with evidence of acute ischemia such as ischemic symptoms, ECG changes, imaging, or coronary thrombus. Chronic kidney disease is one setting in which troponin may be chronically elevated.
questions.source_name: AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF — Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction
questions.source_detail: Troponin elevation means myocardial injury; diagnosis of MI requires clinical evidence of acute ischemia and integrated biomarker/ECG/clinical assessment.
